title: Dottie and Rook's Lost Compass
markdown:
Dottie the dolphin had a gleam in her eye and a wiggle in her tail that said let’s go. Her best mate was Rook the reef goby, no bigger than a thumb, with eyes that missed nothing, including knots that were not as tight as Dottie claimed. Together they zipped near the Great Coral City, a rainbow underwater, where even the shadows seemed to have been painted on purpose.

Dottie had a treasure: not a coin or a pirate’s hat, but a Pearl Compass. It looked like a perfect shimmering pearl, and when you held it just right a tiny arrow inside pointed wherever your heart truly wanted to go. It belonged to Finley Finnegan, a mer-person in a palace of shells and sea glass, who had lent it for safekeeping.

“Keep it safe, Dottie,” Finley had said, tail fanning. “It guides me home when I explore too far.”

Dottie promised. She really promised. She kept it in a pouch of woven seaweed, tied with the strongest kelp she could find, snug against her side. The knot, if she was honest, was a tiny bit loose. She was always in a hurry to swim. Rook had watched her tie it and had not said, in so many words, that hurry and kelp were not friends. His eyes had said it anyway.

Then a flurry of fins. A school of giggling clownfish, playing Tag the Tentacle, whizzed too close, orange and white and entirely without brakes. One bumped her hard, a squashy little crash. The pouch popped. The Pearl Compass flew, arrow spinning like a mad firefly that had forgotten which way was home.

“Flippers.” Dottie’s cheerful squeak went worried.

It bounced off a knobby starfish, rolled over waving sea grass, and with a tiny tink vanished into a swirling coral tunnel. A mischievous current grabbed it deep into a maze of arches, the sort of maze that thinks it is funny.

“Rook, we’ve got to get it back.” Heart flip-flop. Smile gone. Determined frown. The hurry that had tied the knot was now a hurry of a different kind.

Rook, from a perch on brain coral, puffed his chest until he was almost two thumbs. “Aye aye, Captain Dottie. Lead the way. Eyes peeled for trouble. And the compass. And any more clownfish with no manners.”

The current was a playful giant hand through rainbow coral. Fast. Sunny shallows dappled like confetti, then shadowy grottos where silver fish flashed like living glitter. Dottie wanted to outswim the problem. Rook wanted to notice it. That was how they usually won, when they remembered both jobs.

“Watch out,” Rook squeaked. “Incoming grumpy.”

Prickles Puffington the pufferfish blocked the archway, bristly as a badly knitted jumper, grumbling from somewhere inside his own spikes. “Nobody swims through my arch without a toll of one particularly shiny pebble. Make it snappy. I have puffing to do.”

Dottie slowed, which for Dottie was an event. “We don’t have pebbles. We lost a Pearl Compass.”

Prickles wobbled his spines. “No pebbles, no pass. Off you puff.”

Rook scanned the seafloor, wiggled, zipped down, and with surprising strength grabbed a perfectly round smooth grey stone. It was not shiny. It was extremely round, which Rook clearly hoped would count as a personality. “Here you go. It’s very round.”

Prickles eyed pebble, Rook, Dottie. A grunt of grudging approval. Spines relaxed a notch. “Hmph. Fine. Go.”

They zoomed through. “Thanks, Rook. You’re a genius.” Dottie did a little somersault.

“Just observant, Captain.”

The current pulled deeper. Sea fans swayed like gossiping aunties. Dottie gasped. “It’s leading somewhere important. The compass must be close.” She almost charged. Rook finned in front of her nose, a tiny blue-and-yellow stop sign.

“Pouch check,” he said.

Dottie checked. The kelp ends still dangled like unbrushed hair. She made a face. “After,” she said. “After we have it.”

They emerged into a deep cavern lit by star-like algae. On a mossy rock sat a massive sea turtle: Silas the Sage, oldest in these waters, shell encrusted with ancient barnacles, eyes holding a thousand tides. Beside him pulsed the Pearl Compass, gentle and familiar, as if it had been waiting for someone who would not snatch.

“Halt, little swimmers.” Silas’s voice was pebbles in surf. “You seek the compass. The sea does not give up treasures easily. Prove your worthiness.”

They swam closer, buzzing. So close. Dottie’s nose wanted the pearl. Her hurry sat up like a clownfish.

“Answer this riddle. I have cities, but no houses. I have mountains, but no trees. I have water, but no fish. What am I?”

Dottie tilted her head, clicks buzzing, a whole clicky argument with herself. Rook’s tiny brain whirred. Impossible, on the face of it. Cities without houses sounded like a trick, and Dottie disliked tricks that slowed a chase.

“Sometimes,” Dottie whispered, “the answer is right in front of you, just not the way you expect. Think about what Silas is doing.”

Rook looked at the compass, at Silas, around the cavern, at the star-algae that were not stars. “I know. It’s a map.”

Silas’s eyes twinkled. “Clever. You see the world not only as it is, but as it can be pictured. Take it. Remember: adventure is the journey and the friends you travel with.” He nudged the compass toward them, slow as a tide that had decided to be kind.

Dottie tucked it into the pouch and tied the kelp twice this time, tight enough to mean it, tight enough that Rook’s eyes approved. A grateful nod, a flick of tails. The current, now a helpful friend, carried them back through the arches. Prickles had fallen asleep in a roundish way and did not even charge a second pebble.

Finley’s clam palace sparkled. He had been pacing, which in a mer-person looks like a worried waltz. When he saw the compass safe, his face lit brighter than a thousand jellyfish. “You found it.” A bubbly hug, sea salt and sunshine.

Dottie and Rook beamed. Grumpy puffer, coral maze, a turtle’s riddle. The smallest fish had been observant. The fastest dolphin had learned a tighter knot. Another splash of adventure would wait; for now the palace lamps, the pouch snug, and two friends hanging in the easy blue were treasure enough.
